chapter.title: Rexx Classes that Extend Python Classes
chapter.para: A Rexx class can extend a Python class, so that Python calls the Rexx methods where it would call the class's own. Many Python libraries are used that way: a threading.Thread whose run is the program's, an html.parser.HTMLParser whose handle_starttag is, a sequence that implements __len__ and __getitem__. The Rexx class itself is the subclass, as with .js~extend in ooRexx/WASM and .net~extend in ooRexx/.NET.
The class is a subclass of PyObject, and calls .py~extend(self, base) () once: its activate class method is the natural place. Its init passes the arguments to the base with self~init:super(...).

example.title: A Rexx class that extends a Python class
example.programlisting:
g = .Polite~new("Ann") say g~greet -- Greeter.greet calls the override say g~both say .py~isinstance(g, .Polite~pyClass) .py~type(g)~getattr("__name__") say (.py~list((g,))[0] == g) -- back from Python: the object itself
::class Polite subclass PyObject ::method activate class .py~exec("class Greeter:" || "0a"x ||, " def __init__(self, name): self.name = name" || "0a"x ||, " def greeting(self): return 'Hello'" || "0a"x ||, " def greet(self): return self.greeting() + ', ' + self.name") .py~extend(self, .py~main~Greeter) ::method init use arg name self~init:super(name) -- Greeter(name) ::method greeting -- overrides Greeter.greeting return "Good morning" ::method both return self~greeting "/" self~greeting:super -- the override, the base's own
::requires "python.cls"
example.screen: Good morning, Ann Good morning / Hello 1 POLITE 1

section.title: What Is Overridden
section.para: Every method of the Rexx class, and of its superclasses below PyObject, overrides the base's, except init, uninit, unknown, private methods and names with a dot. The methods are looked at when extend runs. A method's Python name is:

listitem.para: the name an annotation gives: ::annotate method do_get python "do_GET";
else, for a __dunder__ name, the lowercase one;

section.para: When two of the base's attributes match (foo and FOO), it is an error that asks for the annotation. __new__, __init__, __del__ and Python's attribute machinery (__getattribute__, __setattr__...) cannot be overridden: the Rexx class's init and uninit do that work.

section.title: How Python Calls a Rexx Method
section.para: Python calls an override with its positional arguments, and with a as the last argument when it passes keyword arguments: kw["by"]. self is the Rexx object. The result goes to Python by , but special methods convert it as Python requires: a Rexx 0 from __bool__ is False, a "7" from __len__ is 7, a 42 from __repr__ is '42'.
A Python exception raised in the method, by Python code it calls or by , and not trapped, reaches the Python caller as itself: a sequence ends with IndexError, an iterator with StopIteration.

example.title: A Python sequence written in Rexx
example.programlisting:
s = .Squares~new say .py~list(s) .py~len(s) .py~eval("lambda s: 4 in s")~new(s)
::class Squares subclass PyObject ::method activate class .py~extend(self, "collections.abc.Sequence") ::method init self~init:super ::method __len__ return 4 ::method __getitem__ use arg i if i >= 4 then .py~raise(.py~IndexError, i) -- the end, for Python return i * i
::requires "python.cls"

example.title: An override called with keyword arguments
example.programlisting:
k = .Show~new .py~eval("lambda o: o.call(3, by=4)")~new(k)
::class Show subclass PyObject ::method activate class .py~exec("class Base:" || "0a"x || " def call(self, x, by=1): return x * by") .py~extend(self, .py~main~Base) ::method init self~init:super ::method call use arg x, kw say "x" x "by" kw["by"]
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Making Objects
section.para: .MyClass~new(args) makes the Rexx object; its init calls self~init:super(args), which runs the base's __new__ and __init__ with them. Until then there is no Python object. Immutable bases (str, int, tuple) take their value there, so init can compute it: self~init:super("<" || name || ">"). A base constructor that calls an override reaches the Rexx method.

Python code that makes one itself (MyClass(...), json.dumps(x, cls=...), a socketserver making its handlers) gets the same: the Rexx object, its init, then the Python object. gives the Python class to hand to such code.

example.title: Extending an immutable class
example.programlisting:
t = .Tag~new("b") say t .py~len(t) .py~type(t)~getattr("__name__") t~upper (t~class == .Tag)
::class Tag subclass PyObject ::method activate class .py~extend(self, "str") ::method init use arg name self~init:super("<" || name || ">") -- the str's value
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: The Base's Members, and Identity
section.para: self~name:super(args), in a method of the class, is the base's own member, not the override. A member that is not overridden is reached as with any PyObject: c~name.

The Python object comes back to Rexx as the Rexx object itself, even when its base is str or int: .py~list((c,))[0] == c, and it is an instance of the Rexx class. The Python class that extend makes is named as the Rexx class.

section.title: Lifetime
section.para: The Rexx object and its Python object are a pair, which lives while Rexx holds the one or Python holds the other, and the two garbage collectors release it as they release everything else: nothing needs a hand. Each collector sees only its own side, so the bridge lets the link that keeps the other half alive point one way at a time. While Rexx holds the Rexx object, it holds its Python object. When Rexx no longer does, the bridge holds the Rexx object, and the Python object is held by Python alone, so that Python's collector decides: if Python no longer holds it either, the pair is over; if Python hands it to Rexx again, Rexx holds it again.

The class's uninit, if it has one, runs once, when the pair is over, not when only Rexx lets it go; the Python object is gone by then. A Rexx class that extends a Python class, and the Python class it makes, are released as any class is.

section.title: Threads
section.para: Python may call the overrides on any of its threads; the threading.Thread example in ooRexx and Python: Cookbook runs its Rexx run method on the thread Python starts. Several at once need ooRexx 5.3.0 (see ).
